paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn recommendations for many users together when feedback can be adversarial. Each user has a separate multi-armed bandit problem: the learner chooses among items and receives limited feedback. An adversary can choose both which user appears and the losses presented. The learner also knows the strengths of social connections between users.

The central assumption is that strongly connected users tend to prefer the same action. The authors express this through a resistance-based measure of how smoothly a user-to-action assignment varies across the network. Their algorithms, GABA-I and GABA-II, favor assignments with low dispersion, allowing social structure to guide learning across users.

The two algorithms offer different trade-offs. GABA-I has the stronger expected regret guarantee, while GABA-II processes each interaction faster, particularly as the number of items grows. The analysis identifies improvements over learning independently for every user. Those benefits are expressed through the network dispersion measure, connecting the guarantees to how well users’ preferred actions align with their social links.
neurips-2021-a-gang-of-adversarial-bandi.tldr: Two bandit algorithms use social connections to share learning across users, with different trade-offs between regret guarantees and computation.

paragraphs: Attacking a video classifier through queries alone requires finding input changes that make it misclassify a video. Video adds a temporal dimension to this search, making useful gradient estimates harder to obtain than for images. The paper investigates whether structure across time can reduce the number of queries needed to find effective perturbations.

The proposed method, GEO-TRAP, describes the temporal progression of candidate gradients using geometric transformations. Instead of searching directly across the full space of possible gradients, its iterative procedure searches over a small set of transformation parameters. This produces a smaller, structured search space while retaining directions that can lead to successful attacks.

On the Jester dataset, the authors report better attack success rates with approximately 73.55% fewer queries than the compared state-of-the-art video attack. Across two large datasets, they report new state-of-the-art black-box results and vulnerabilities in diverse video classifiers. These findings show that geometric structure can make query-based video attacks substantially more efficient in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-adversarial-attacks-on-blac.tldr: GEO-TRAP uses geometric transformations to structure video attack searches, achieving stronger attacks with substantially fewer queries in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Private inference uses cryptographic operations to run a neural network while protecting user privacy, but those operations can impose substantial computational costs. This paper focuses on a mismatch between ordinary inference optimization and private inference: reducing arithmetic work does not directly address the expensive ReLU operations that dominate the latter setting.

Circa reworks a ReLU computation as an approximate test of whether a value is positive. A new truncation method makes that sign test cheaper, producing a particular form of stochastic ReLU. The approach rests on the observation that the resulting pattern of occasional errors fits the fault tolerance of neural network inference, allowing cheaper computations without affecting accuracy in the reported results.

The authors demonstrate storage improvements of up to 4.7 times and runtime improvements of up to 3 times over baseline implementations. Applying Circa alongside recent private-inference optimizations yields an additional 1.8-times speedup. These results make the operation being optimized central to the contribution: private inference benefits from targeting its cryptographic bottlenecks directly.
neurips-2021-circa-stochastic-relus-for-.tldr: Circa makes private inference cheaper by replacing expensive ReLU computations with stochastic approximations that preserve accuracy in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Structured neural networks divide computation among components, such as transformer positions, modular slots, or graph nodes. Their connectivity and attention mechanisms already constrain how components communicate. This paper asks whether restricting the messages themselves to discrete representations provides a useful additional learning bias, particularly for systematic generalization.

The proposed discrete-valued neural communication method builds on discretization used in VQ-VAE. It uses multiple discretization heads with shared codebooks at component outputs, so communication draws on common sets of discrete representations. Human communication through symbols supplies a motivating analogy. The paper also presents theoretical results showing increased noise robustness and reduced underlying model dimensionality from discretization.

Experiments report substantial improvements in systematic generalization across transformers, modular architectures, and graph neural networks. The method is also reported to be robust to hyperparameter choices. Together, these findings support the hypothesis that constraining internal communication can help structured models generalize. The language analogy motivates the design; the empirical and theoretical results provide the paper’s evidence for its benefits.
neurips-2021-discrete-valued-neural-comm.tldr: Restricting communication between neural-network components to shared discrete representations improves systematic generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Gradient-based explanations often assume that large input gradients identify features relevant to a particular prediction. This paper tests that assumption directly. The gradients in question describe how a model’s output scores change with its input; interpreting their magnitudes as evidence of discriminative features requires a further claim that the authors put under scrutiny.

Their evaluation framework, DiffROAR, tests this claim on four image-classification benchmarks. The results suggest that standard models can strongly violate the assumption, while adversarially robust models satisfy it in these evaluations. The authors also introduce BlockMNIST, a constructed dataset whose discriminative features are known in advance, to examine and characterize these differences more directly.

A theoretical analysis establishes a corresponding failure for standard one-hidden-layer networks on a simplified BlockMNIST setting: their gradients do not highlight the signal coordinates specific to each instance. This proof has a defined setting rather than universal scope. The combined evidence motivates explicit, falsifiable tests of explanation assumptions and positions the proposed framework and datasets as possible interpretability audits.
neurips-2021-do-input-gradients-highligh.tldr: Experiments and a simplified theoretical analysis challenge the assumption that standard models’ input gradients identify instance-specific discriminative features.

paragraphs: A robot’s performance depends on both its physical design and the controller that makes it move. Evolution Gym provides a large-scale benchmark for optimizing these together. The paper addresses the difficulty of comparing methods for this joint problem, where changing a robot’s body also changes what an effective controller must learn.

Robots are assembled from modular voxels with different properties, including soft material, rigid material, and actuators. Tasks cover movement across different terrains and manipulation. The authors combine design-optimization methods with deep reinforcement learning to create and evaluate several algorithms that evolve robot bodies alongside their control strategies.

As evolution progresses, the evaluated robots develop more complex behavior, and the best designs solve many tasks. Designs created from scratch often resemble natural creatures and outperform hand-designed robots. However, every tested algorithm fails on the hardest environments. The benchmark therefore supplies both evidence that joint optimization can produce effective designs and concrete challenges that remain unsolved by the evaluated methods.
neurips-2021-evolution-gym-a-large-scale.tldr: Evolution Gym benchmarks joint robot-body and controller optimization, producing capable evolved robots while exposing tasks that defeat all tested algorithms.

paragraphs: Automated hyperparameter optimization can find strong model configurations without clearly explaining how different settings affect performance. This paper uses the experimental data gathered during Bayesian optimization to build such explanations. Its focus is partial dependence plots, which summarize how predicted performance changes with a hyperparameter while averaging over other settings.

A difficulty is that Bayesian optimization preferentially samples promising configurations. Its collected data therefore cover some regions much better than others, creating a risk of biased interpretations. The authors use the posterior uncertainty of the optimization surrogate model to attach estimated confidence bands to partial dependence plots, making uncertainty part of the explanation.

They also partition the hyperparameter space and construct plots within relevant subregions. This seeks more reliable local explanations where the available evidence supports greater confidence. An experimental study provides quantitative evidence that plots within these subregions improve in quality. The contribution connects optimization and explanation by using both the surrogate’s predictions and its uncertainty to interpret an unevenly sampled search space.
neurips-2021-explaining-hyperparameter-o.tldr: Uncertainty-aware partial dependence plots and targeted subregions improve explanations of Bayesian hyperparameter optimization in the reported study.

paragraphs: Meta-learning must generalize at two levels: a learner adapts using data within a task, while a meta-learner learns across tasks. This paper seeks useful performance guarantees for gradient-based meta-learning, motivated by earlier bounds that can be difficult to evaluate or too loose to say much even in relatively simple settings.

The authors combine different mathematical tools for the two levels. Uniform stability controls generalization of the base learning algorithm, while PAC-Bayes analysis handles the meta level. Their resulting probability-based guarantee becomes tighter when the base learner adapts quickly. That relationship is especially relevant because rapid adaptation is itself a central aim of meta-learning.

The bound gives tighter guarantees than compared alternatives on a toy non-convex problem on the unit sphere and a text-classification example. The authors also derive a practical regularization scheme and report improved performance over baseline techniques. This scheme is evaluated even where the bound remains loose, distinguishing a useful training idea motivated by theory from a claim that the guarantee is always informative.
neurips-2021-generalization-bounds-for-m.tldr: Combining stability and PAC-Bayes analysis yields meta-learning guarantees that tighten with fast adaptation and motivates an effective regularization scheme.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals aim to contain the true outcome at a chosen rate. Conditional coverage asks for that rate across different regions of the input space, so overall coverage alone is insufficient. Quantile regression approaches the desired coverage in the large-sample limit, but the authors find that its finite-sample conditional coverage can be poor.

The proposed method modifies the quantile-regression loss to encourage independence between interval width and whether an interval misses its outcome. For the true conditional quantiles, these quantities are independent. Encouraging this relationship therefore adds a criterion that remains compatible with the target quantiles while addressing an observable pattern associated with uneven coverage.

Experiments show improved conditional coverage according to several metrics. The paper also introduces two measures that examine dependence between interval size and missed outcomes. These measures connect evaluation to the same relationship used during training. The stated improvement is empirical: the large-sample property of quantile regression and the validity of the modified loss do not themselves establish exact finite-sample coverage everywhere.
neurips-2021-improving-conditional-cover.tldr: A quantile-regression loss that discourages dependence between interval width and prediction misses empirically improves conditional coverage.

paragraphs: Knowledge-graph completion predicts missing triples that describe relationships between entities. Many embedding methods learn vectors for entities encountered during training and score possible triples using a predefined function. This works in a transductive setting, but those approaches cannot directly handle the inductive setting in which new entities appear or graphs are merged.

INDIGO proposes a graph-neural-network approach to this problem. The knowledge graph is fully encoded into the network in a transparent way, and predicted triples can be read directly from its final layer. This makes graph processing itself responsible for producing completion predictions, without an additional scoring function or separate prediction components.

The authors contrast this design with earlier GNN approaches that retain heuristic elements and ad-hoc scoring functions. Their experiments show better performance than state-of-the-art methods on inductive graph-completion benchmarks. The result supports an architectural route to predicting relationships involving newly introduced entities: encode the graph for the GNN so that its output directly expresses the triples being predicted.
neurips-2021-indigo-gnn-based-inductive-.tldr: INDIGO encodes knowledge graphs into a GNN that directly predicts missing triples and outperforms compared methods on inductive completion benchmarks.

paragraphs: Survival models predict the timing of events when some outcomes are censored, meaning their event time is not fully observed. Models trained by maximum likelihood may perform poorly on evaluation criteria such as Brier score or Bernoulli log likelihood at selected time horizons, because training does not directly optimize those criteria.

Direct optimization creates a circular dependency. Correcting a failure-model objective for censoring requires a censoring distribution, while estimating the censoring model under these criteria requires the failure distribution. Inverse-Weighted Survival Games couples the two models: each objective uses reweighted estimates based on the other model, which is held fixed while that objective is trained.

For proper losses, the authors prove that the true failure and censoring distributions form a stationary point: once there, the game does not move away. They establish uniqueness in one constructed case, without claiming universal convergence to that point. Simulations show Brier-score optimization, and applications to cancer and critically ill patient data demonstrate the approach in real-world survival settings.
neurips-2021-inverse-weighted-survival-g.tldr: Coupled survival and censoring models enable direct training for evaluation losses, with the true distributions forming a stationary point under proper losses.

paragraphs: Topic models are often evaluated using automated coherence scores based on how frequently topic words occur together in a reference corpus. Neural models have surpassed classical models on these scores. This paper asks whether those apparent gains correspond to human judgments, since coherence measures developed for classical models had not been validated through human experiments for neural models.

The authors identify two separate problems. A literature meta-analysis reveals inconsistent benchmark practices, while the lack of human validation leaves the meaning of automated improvements uncertain. They compare coherence scores with topic-rating and word-intrusion judgments, and systematically evaluate one prominent classical model and two leading neural models on two commonly used datasets.

The automated evaluations select a winning model where the corresponding human evaluations do not. This discrepancy challenges the practice of treating coherence scores alone as decisive evidence of topic-model quality. The finding concerns a mismatch in the evaluated comparisons; it supports grounding automatic evaluation in human judgments rather than assuming that score advantages necessarily establish better topics.
neurips-2021-is-automated-topic-model-ev.tldr: Automated topic-coherence scores identify winners that human evaluations do not, challenging their use as standalone evidence of model quality.

paragraphs: This paper studies how adding connections to an existing social network can reduce a combined measure of polarization and disagreement. The decision is to recommend a fixed number of new links. Existing opinions and the starting network provide the setting, so the optimization concerns which additional relationships would most improve the stated objective.

The authors show that the objective is monotone but not submodular. These properties distinguish predictable improvement from the stronger diminishing-returns structure often useful in network optimization. They develop a simple greedy algorithm with a constant-factor approximation guarantee and cubic running time, providing a theoretical bound on its solution quality.

To handle larger networks, they also propose a faster algorithm whose stated complexity scales with the existing edge count, the number of recommended links, and an inverse-squared accuracy parameter, apart from logarithmic factors in network size. Experiments on real datasets demonstrate efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution combines a formal link-selection objective with algorithms intended to make that objective computationally manageable.
neurips-2021-minimizing-polarization-and.tldr: The paper develops theoretically supported algorithms for selecting new social links to reduce a combined polarization-and-disagreement objective.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses previously collected data to improve a decision-making policy. This paper considers data generated by a known baseline policy in an environment with multiple reward signals. Each reward defines an objective, so improvement requires handling trade-offs among outcomes while accounting for uncertainty about the consequences of a new policy.

The proposed formulation incorporates the user’s preferences over those trade-offs while requiring the new policy to perform at least as well as the baseline on every individual objective. The authors build a method on Safe Policy Iteration with Baseline Bootstrapping and provide high-probability performance guarantees for the true environment. The guarantees are probabilistic rather than unconditional assurances.

The method is evaluated on a synthetic grid-world safety task and a critical-care problem involving policies for IV fluids and vasopressors in sepsis treatment. The abstract reports effectiveness in these settings. Its central contribution is making user-directed optimization compatible with separate baseline protections, so favorable performance on one objective does not by itself justify deterioration on another.
neurips-2021-multi-objective-spibb-seldo.tldr: Multi-Objective SPIBB uses offline data to pursue user preferences while providing high-probability baseline-performance protections for each objective.

paragraphs: Multi-view graph clustering seeks groups of nodes using several sources of graph and attribute information. Existing approaches often emphasize either multiple graphs or multiple views of attributes. This paper proposes a general framework for multi-view attributed graphs, with particular attention to the fact that an original graph may be noisy or incomplete.

The method, MCGC, first filters the graph information to suppress unwanted high-frequency noise while preserving geometric features. This produces smoother node representations. It then learns a consensus graph using a graph-contrastive loss as a regularizer. The learned graph brings the views together and supplies structure for clustering when the original graph is not directly suitable.

Results on several benchmark datasets show improvements over compared state-of-the-art approaches, including existing deep-learning methods. These findings support the combination of graph filtering and contrastive consensus learning in the evaluated tasks. The paper’s contribution is a relatively simple two-step route from imperfect, multi-view input to a graph representation that better supports clustering.
neurips-2021-multi-view-contrastive-grap.tldr: MCGC combines graph filtering with contrastive consensus-graph learning to improve clustering of multi-view attributed graphs.

paragraphs: Models often lose accuracy when tested in environments different from those used for training. This paper connects that problem to calibration: whether a classifier’s confidence agrees with how often it is correct. The authors focus on calibration across several domains and relate it to the invariant representations commonly pursued for out-of-domain generalization.

Their theoretical result shows that, under certain conditions, models calibrated across multiple domains are free of spurious correlations. This motivates multi-domain calibration as a measurable, trainable surrogate for performance in unseen domains. The authors introduce methods for improving it either while training a model or by modifying an existing one.

Experiments use four datasets from the WILDS benchmark and Colored MNIST. Training or tuning for calibration across domains significantly improves performance on unseen test domains in these evaluations. The evidence combines a conditional theoretical connection with practical improvements. It does not make calibration an unconditional guarantee of transfer, but identifies a concrete property that can help guide efforts to improve it.
neurips-2021-on-calibration-and-out-of-d.tldr: Multi-domain calibration has a conditional theoretical link to avoiding spurious correlations and improves unseen-domain performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient algorithms improve reinforcement-learning policies using estimated gradients. Variance reduction can make these estimates more useful, but the paper identifies a theoretical obstacle: existing variance-reduced methods rely on an importance-weight assumption that must hold at every iteration and cannot be checked. The authors introduce a simple gradient-truncation mechanism to address this issue.

Their algorithm, TSIVR-PG, supports both cumulative reward maximization and more general utilities defined over a policy’s long-term visiting distribution. The latter describes where the policy spends its time. This broadens the optimization target beyond a sum of rewards while retaining a variance-reduced policy-gradient approach.

The analysis gives a sample complexity of approximately epsilon to the power of minus three, up to logarithmic factors, for finding an epsilon-stationary policy. With an additional overparameterization assumption and the problem’s hidden convexity, the authors prove convergence to a globally epsilon-optimal policy using approximately epsilon to the power of minus two samples. The stronger global result therefore depends on extra structure beyond the stationarity guarantee.
neurips-2021-on-the-convergence-and-samp.tldr: TSIVR-PG uses gradient truncation to address an uncheckable importance-weight assumption and establishes stationary-point and conditional global-optimality sample bounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies online optimization when an adversary may choose the loss functions, but those functions reach the learner in a uniformly random order. The learner must make decisions as losses arrive. Random ordering supplies useful structure without requiring the collection of losses itself to have been generated independently from a probability distribution.

The analysis focuses on settings where the cumulative loss is convex or strongly convex, even though individual losses need only be smooth and may be non-convex. The authors develop algorithms with optimal bounds, improving earlier results by eliminating dependence on dimension and obtaining better scaling with the strong-convexity parameter. These gains concern the stated random-order setting.

The proof connects algorithmic stability with generalization under sampling without replacement, alongside a refined average-stability analysis of stochastic gradient descent. Stability concerns how sensitive a learning procedure is to changes in its data. Establishing these connections helps explain how randomly ordered losses can yield strong guarantees even when individual losses lack convexity.
neurips-2021-optimal-rates-for-random-or.tldr: The paper proves optimal dimension-independent bounds for random-order online optimization with convex cumulative loss and potentially non-convex individual losses.

paragraphs: Optimizing competing objectives requires finding useful trade-offs rather than a single best value. Bayesian optimization can select informative evaluations, but noisy observations make it uncertain which trade-offs are currently best. This paper introduces NEHVI, an acquisition function that accounts for uncertainty in the Pareto frontier when calculating expected hypervolume improvement.

The authors show how the same perspective supports selecting several candidates in parallel: even without observation noise, pending evaluations create uncertainty about the frontier. Their batch method, qNEHVI, reduces the computational complexity of parallel expected hypervolume improvement from exponential to polynomial in batch size. They also show how to optimize it with gradients using sample average approximation.

qNEHVI is one-step Bayes-optimal for hypervolume maximization in both noisy and noiseless settings. That claim concerns the next decision under the Bayesian criterion. Experiments report substantially greater noise robustness than existing multi-objective Bayesian-optimization approaches, state-of-the-art optimization performance, and competitive runtimes for large batches. The contribution combines uncertainty handling with a more tractable way to choose parallel evaluations.
neurips-2021-parallel-bayesian-optimizat.tldr: NEHVI and qNEHVI account for uncertain trade-offs to improve noisy multi-objective optimization and make parallel candidate selection computationally cheaper.

paragraphs: In a reward-mixing decision process, a reward model is selected at the start of each episode, but the agent is not told which one was chosen. This hidden choice makes the problem partially observable: the information directly available to the agent does not reveal the full latent state that determines the process.

The paper studies efficient learning when there are two possible reward models. Unlike approaches requiring strong assumptions on the dynamics, it treats this reward-mixing setting without such additional restrictions. The authors develop new exploration and analysis ideas to handle the hidden reward-model identity and provide a polynomial-time algorithm for finding a near-optimal policy.

The episode bound is polynomial in the time horizon and inverse target accuracy, with quadratic dependence on the numbers of states and actions, up to logarithmic factors. The contribution establishes efficient learning in a partially observed setting whose observation space is smaller than its latent state space. Its scope is the specified two-model reward-mixing problem, rather than arbitrary partially observable environments.
neurips-2021-reinforcement-learning-in-r.tldr: The paper gives a polynomial-time near-optimal learning algorithm for reward-mixing processes with two hidden reward models and unrestricted dynamics.

paragraphs: Spatial networks combine connectivity with geometry: nodes and edges occupy real space, and that geometry affects network structure. This paper develops representations that bring those sources of information together. A central requirement is that arbitrary node ordering, rotation, or translation should not determine how the network is represented.

The authors introduce a spatial-information representation that is provably information-lossless and invariant to rotation and translation. They then design a higher-order spatial network convolution suited to that representation. This pairs an explicit treatment of geometry with a network-processing operation, addressing the need to capture spatial relationships and connectivity within one framework.

To improve efficiency, the method samples random spanning trees, reducing the stated time and memory complexity from cubic to linear in network size. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the framework’s strength. The contribution combines a theoretical representation property, a compatible learning operation, and a computational simplification, making preservation of spatial information and efficient network learning parts of the same design.
neurips-2021-representation-learning-on-.tldr: The framework combines invariant spatial representations with network convolutions and spanning-tree sampling to learn efficiently from geometry and connectivity.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of Gaussian latent-tree structures from vector observations when some observations may be arbitrarily corrupted. It addresses both how many samples existing algorithms require and how to modify them to withstand corrupted data. Hidden variables make structure recovery harder because the full tree cannot be observed directly.

The authors analyze Recursive Grouping and Chow-Liu Recursive Grouping without an earlier bounded-effective-depth assumption. For the hidden Markov model case, they show that Chow-Liu initialization reduces dependence on tree diameter from exponential to logarithmic. They also use truncated inner products to robustify these algorithms and two neighbor-joining methods.

The robust algorithms tolerate a corruption count up to the square root of the number of clean samples. The paper additionally derives an instance-dependent impossibility result, describing limits on latent-tree structure learning. Comparing sample requirements with that lower bound verifies the stated optimality of robust Chow-Liu Recursive Grouping and Neighbor Joining. These results tie robustness guarantees to both algorithm design and fundamental data requirements.
neurips-2021-robustifying-algorithms-of-.tldr: Truncated inner products make latent-tree learning algorithms tolerate bounded corruption, while new sample-complexity and impossibility results establish theoretical performance limits.

paragraphs: Transformer self-attention has quadratic time and memory costs, making training expensive as the number of elements grows. This paper draws on approximation methods from kernel machines, which face a related bottleneck from computing pairwise relationships. The aim is to reduce attention’s computational burden while retaining useful predictive performance.

Skyformer replaces the usual softmax structure with a Gaussian kernel to stabilize training. It then adapts the Nyström approximation method to a matrix that is not positive semidefinite, accelerating computation. These are linked design choices: the attention formulation changes, and a kernel-based approximation supplies the mechanism for computing it more cheaply.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis showing small matrix-approximation error in spectral norm. Experiments on the Long Range Arena benchmark find performance comparable to, or better than, full self-attention while using fewer computational resources. The theoretical result characterizes the approximation, while the benchmark results support its practical usefulness for the evaluated tasks. Together they motivate borrowing kernel-computation techniques when redesigning efficient attention.
neurips-2021-skyformer-remodel-self-atte.tldr: Skyformer combines Gaussian-kernel attention with a Nyström approximation to reduce computation while matching or improving benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Person re-identification involves matching images of people, making relationships between two images central to the task. This paper investigates transformers for image matching and metric learning. The authors find that the evaluated Vision Transformer and standard decoder-based transformer are inadequate for this purpose because they lack the needed image-to-image attention.

They test concatenating query and gallery inputs and adding cross-attention between them. Cross-attention improves performance, but the gains remain limited. TransMatcher instead simplifies the decoder: it retains query-key similarity calculations, removes the full softmax-weighted attention operation, and uses global max pooling plus a multilayer perceptron to produce the matching result.

The simplified decoder is reported to be both more computationally efficient and more effective for matching. On several popular generalizable person-re-identification datasets, TransMatcher achieves state-of-the-art results, with gains up to 6.1% in Rank-1 and 5.7% in mAP. The findings support designing the transformer’s comparison mechanism around pairwise matching, rather than assuming that attention built for global feature aggregation will already serve that purpose well.
neurips-2021-transmatcher-deep-image-mat.tldr: TransMatcher simplifies transformer decoding around image-pair similarities, improving efficiency and generalizable person-re-identification performance.

paragraphs: Whole-slide pathology classification can use multiple instance learning to learn from slide-level supervision. A slide contains multiple instances whose relationships may carry useful information. This paper challenges the common assumption that those instances are independent and identically distributed, arguing that it neglects correlations within the slide.

The authors propose a correlated multiple-instance-learning framework and provide a convergence proof. Their transformer-based implementation, TransMIL, incorporates both morphological and spatial information. This allows the classification process to consider what instances look like and how they relate spatially. The method is reported to handle balanced and unbalanced data, binary and multiclass tasks, and to offer useful visualization and interpretability.

Experiments across three computational-pathology problems show better performance and faster convergence than compared state-of-the-art methods. Reported test AUCs reach 93.09% on CAMELYON16 for binary tumor classification and 96.03% and 98.82% on TCGA-NSCLC and TCGA-RCC for cancer-subtype classification. These results support explicitly modeling instance correlations when learning slide-level predictions from weak supervision.
neurips-2021-transmil-transformer-based-.tldr: TransMIL models correlations among whole-slide image instances using morphological and spatial information, improving classification and convergence in three pathology evaluations.
